articles.title: ICC prosecutors want to admit 3 pre-recorded testimonies on Duterte's 'narco-list'
articles.summary: PRAGUE, Czech Republic - To expedite the proceedings in Rodrigo Duterte"s case before the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Office of the Prosecutor seeks to admit three pre-recorded witness…

blocks.text: PRAGUE, Czech Republic – To expedite the proceedings in Rodrigo Duterte’s case before the International Criminal Court (ICC), the Office of the Prosecutor seeks to admit three pre-recorded witness testimonies regarding the former president’s “narco list.”

In a redacted request for application filed on November 2, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang requested Trial Chamber III to admit the prior recorded testimonies of witnesses P-1097, P-1170, and P-1318, which are “relevant” proof of Duterte’s “individual criminal liability”, particularly in identifying “high-value targets” on various drug watch lists.
The prosecution added that these statements also establish the Philippine National Police’s (PNP) role in Duterte’s drug war.

Niang stated that the prior recorded testimonies are introduced via the ICC’s Rule of Procedure and Evidence Rule 68(3), which may allow admission of such statements in proceedings while the witness appears in court and does not object.
Recorded testimonies

Although heavily redacted, the three witnesses’ statements, as the prosecution noted, establish the targeting of individuals by PNP officers during Duterte’s drug war, as well as “the shift in [REDACTED] after Mr Duterte became President.”
P-1097’s prior recorded testimony explains the “tokhang” killings and that “warning placards were placed on some victims.”
The prosecution noted that P-1170’s testimony demonstrates Duterte’s public accusation of redacted individuals as being involved with illegal drugs, who were later included on the “PRRD list.”

The pre-recorded testimony of P-1318 is heavily redacted, but the prosecution said it describes the Operation Double Barrel and the tokhang killings, including “some police killings [that] were staged through nanlaban narratives, evidence planting, and cover-ups.”

The prosecution noted that it would conduct a “limited and focused supplementary examination” of the witnesses – all referred to in the filing with male pronouns – should their prior recorded testimonies be introduced as evidence.
It also seeks to use associated materials for P-1097, P-1170, and P-1318 as evidence “necessary to fully comprehend” their accounts.

The filing noted that the three witnesses’ statements “are internally consistent, mutually corroborative, and accompanied by supporting documents in relation to certain aspects,” and that they corroborate the evidence to be provided by other viva voce witnesses.
'Paper-only' witness

Meanwhile, Duterte’s defense counsel, Peter Haynes, is asking Trial Chamber III to reject the prosecution’s application to admit witness P-1357’s prior recorded testimony under Rule 68(2), which would allow the statement in court without the witness’s appearance.
In a redacted response filing on the same day, Haynes claims P-1357 “exemplifies the very type of individual whom the Chamber urged the Prosecution to remove from its list.”

“Her testimony is entirely peripheral, as it does not address the substance of [REDACTED] research, the allegations made, or the findings reached. The witness is not even familiar with the events occurring after [REDACTED], having ceased working on the subject following [REDACTED],” Haynes stated.

It may be recalled that the prosecution asked Trial Chamber III on October 19 to admit the prior recorded testimony of P-1357, P-0024, and P-1359 as Rule 68(2)(b) evidence that relates to the alleged systematic policy of “neutralizing” alleged criminals across the Philippines through murder.

The prior recorded testimony of P-1357, referred to in female pronouns, contains details of the existence and operations of the Davao Death Squad and “notes that the words and actions of Mr Duterte indicated his support for killings of criminal suspects.”
But Haynes objected to admitting P-1357’s statement, saying it “adds nothing of substance to the evidence in this case.”

“Further and/or alternatively, the Defence objects to the Prosecution’s improper use of Rule 68(2)(b) to introduce associated material that the witness has neither meaningfully used nor explained, contrary to the Prosecution’s assertions,” Haynes stated.
Haynes said the defense has “no wish” to cross-examine P-1357, “given the marginal relevance of her testimony.”

The defense said it won’t cross-examine P-0024 because of “having already extensively addressed its concerns regarding the introduction of the [REDACTED] dataset into the evidentiary record of these proceedings.”

P-0024’s heavily redacted statement mentions a “legal process,” and “records [that] may have been incomplete or selectively disclosed.” It remains unclear which information P-0024’s statement refers to.
Ramifications, deadlines

At the final status conference, senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls and trial lawyer Edward Jeremy told Trial Chamber III Presiding Judge Joanna Korner that the Office of the Prosecution would submit eight additional applications to admit Rule 68(3) witnesses.

Korner also asked the prosecution and the defense for suggestions on in-court protective measures regarding Rule 68(3) witnesses, citing “various ramifications” and the need for “certainty about the deadlines.”
Earlier, Nichols said that by submitting prior recorded witness statements, they hope to “cut down in half” the six hours allocated to present their opening statements.
The ICC’s trial of Duterte for crimes against humanity is set for November 30. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Thousands of European troops to rehearse Ukraine deployment in event of peace
articles.summary: Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in any offensive operations.

blocks.text: Britain and France are to lead a military exercise to test a multinational force's ability to deploy to Ukraine, if there is a peace deal.
Nearly 3,000 military personnel from 12 European nations will take part in the rehearsal in neighbouring Poland this month.
Plans for a reassurance force for Ukraine were set out last year as one of the long-term security guarantees being proposed by European nations.

But there are still more questions than answers as to how such a military force might work in practice. Western officials stress that any force sent to Ukraine would not take part in offensive operations or be involved in peacekeeping or ceasefire monitoring missions.
Nor would they be operating under the command of Nato or on the front line.
Officials say their presence would be to provide reassurance to Ukraine and to help rebuild its armed forces.
The US has been involved in discussions, but is not contributing to the mission.
Russia has already voiced opposition to foreign troops being stationed in Ukraine and, last year, President Vladimir Putin said they would be "legitimate targets".
Western officials have declined to spell out the rules of engagement if any international troops were to be attacked in Ukraine. Though they say the force would be able to defend itself.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the exercise showed Britain, France and their allies were stepping up preparation for the day when peace came to Ukraine.
He said: "This is not a hypothetical plan, it's a real force, ready to help Ukraine once the fighting stops."

Lt Gen Tom Bateman, the UK commander of the Multi National Force – Ukraine (MNF-U), said the exercise represented an important step in translating political commitments into credible military readiness.
He said it was a "real, capable, readily deployable force that represented a serious commitment from Coalition of the Willing nations to Ukraine's long-term stability and security".

Exercise Koalicja - which takes place from 9-22 November - will be a rehearsal of how to move, protect and supply a force in Ukraine. It will also be a test of their command and control to ensure troops from different countries can work together.
Some 2,800 military personnel will take part across land, sea and air, with the UK contribution including 300 troops and a pair of RAF Typhoons.
Fighter jets will simulate how they would reassure commercial aircraft once Ukraine's skies can be reopened.
Turkey has agreed to lead the maritime mission, with the eventual goal to clear mines and allow the resumption of trade in the Black Sea.
As well as the UK, troops will come from France, Belgium, Estonia, France, Germany, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and Turkey.
However, Western officials could not comment on the final make-up and shape of the force that could be deployed to Ukraine if the fighting stops.
In the past, military experts have suggested that Western nations might have to send tens of thousands of troops to Ukraine to guarantee its security.
Officials acknowledge that the countries' commitment and contributions will depend on the circumstances of a cessation of hostilities and individual nations' political decisions.
It is also unclear what training role Western forces could provide to battle hardened Ukraine.
Ukrainian soldiers are already in high demand training Nato forces - passing on their expertise in drone warfare.
Above all, Russia has shown no sign of wanting to end its war.

articles.title: AI-powered malware ‘highly likely’ to be used to hack UK infrastructure by 2028
articles.summary:
National Cyber Security Centre expects attacks on critical facilities such as power stations, airports and hospitals

AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking…

blocks.text: AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the UK’s power stations, airports and hospitals by 2028, according to the state cybersecurity body.

The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said AI will probably enable a ransomware attack against critical national infrastructure [CNI] between now and 2028. The UK’s definition of CNI covers a range of facilities and services across sectors including energy, transport, defence, food, health and finance.
The warning from the NCSC, part of the GCHQ spy agency, was published in the organisation’s annual review, which also warned that Russia and China will start using AI “routinely” in cyber-attacks.
“It is … highly likely that between now and 2028, AI-powered malware will have been used in a ransomware attack on UK CNI,” said NCSC.
Ransomware has become a cornerstone of the criminal hacker’s repertoire and is a signature ploy of gangs that typically operate out of former Soviet Union states.

After gaining access to a victim’s IT systems, the attackers then encrypt files with bespoke malicious software – or malware – and then demand a payment in cryptocurrency to unlock the crippled systems and return any stolen data. UK ransomware victims include Royal Mail, outsourcing firm Capita and various public bodies, including councils.
AI is set to enhance the ransomware threat by helping attackers with tasks such as scouting targets, locating weaknesses in IT networks and writing malicious code, said the NCSC.

Last month, the government urged Britons to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in order to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency. Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said as the Be Ready campaign was launched that Britain needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
NCSC’s chief executive, Richard Horne, will warn the public in a speech accompanying the review on Tuesday that AI is going to unleash a wave of cyber-attacks imminently.
“In the coming months, we face a real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents,” he will say.
Horne will attribute the threat to the technology’s ability to uncover weaknesses in IT systems that have been “tolerated for far too long”.

An example of AI’s capacity to root out previously undetected vulnerabilities came last month, when the technology helped discover a critical weakness in PHP, a computer language used by almost 70% of the world’s websites.
Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at Surrey University, said NCSC’s warning underlined the need for nation states and companies to access cutting-edge AI technology.
after newsletter promotion

“AI can help people find these flaws and patch them, but if we don’t get the access the bad guys will beat them to it,” he said. So far, leading AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have given some companies advanced access to their most powerful models in order to help them identify serious IT glitches.
Horne will also say in his speech that communications networks used by the British military are subjected to daily attacks that are “persistent” and “sustained”.

Horne will say Russia was one of the perpetrators, but the attacks have deliberately not crossed the line into warfare, with Moscow carrying out “notable campaigns” that “intentionally fall below the threshold of armed conflict as they escalate their attempts at hybrid warfare”.

Horne will add that recent cyber-attacks on supermarket fridges in Europe, which have seen fridge temperatures raised by hackers to more than 50C, are a warning to companies and organisations to invest strongly in cyber resilience.
“For decades we have collectively got away with tech on the cheap,” he will say.

articles.title: B.C. ostrich farm files lawsuit demanding compensation for 37 birds 'missing' after 2025 cull
articles.summary: A year after a controversial ostrich cull in B.C.'s Interior, the owners of Universal Ostrich Farms have filed a lawsuit accusing the federal government of animal cruelty, under-compensation and…

image.caption: An ostrich at the Universal Ostrich farm in Edgewood, B.C., prior to the cull. (Frederic Gagnon/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: British Columbia

A year after a controversial ostrich cull in B.C.'s Interior, the owners of Universal Ostrich Farms have filed a lawsuit accusing the federal government of animal cruelty, under-compensation and preventing the launch of a lucrative commercial enterprise.
Universal Ostrich Farms claims they're owed $200M in projected revenue from diet pill made using ostrich eggs
A B.C. ostrich farm at the centre of a culling controversy that made headlines around the world has filed a lawsuit against the federal government and the B.C. RCMP.

A protracted 10-month legal battle to save Universal Ostrich Farms' bird population in Edgewood, B.C., ended in November last year when more than 300 ostriches were culled in response to an avian flu outbreak that led to the deaths of 70 birds.
The farm's owners Karen Espersen and Dave Bilinski had argued the cull was unnecessary because the remaining flock was healthy and had herd immunity.

The notice, filed in the Supreme Court Friday on behalf of Universal Ostrich Farms Inc. and its owner Landco Ventures makes a number of claims against the Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) and RCMP, including an allegation that during quarantine and slaughter operations, 37 ostriches went missing and remain unaccounted for.
"CFIA failed to maintain a proper and comprehensive inventory of all animals in its custody," the notice says.

items: More stories from the B.C. Interior

blocks.text: It says Espersen and Bilinski were offered compensation of $3,000 per bird for 314 birds — a total of $942,000.
"At the time CFIA exercised the warrants 351 birds were located on the property," it reads.
"The full extent of missing birds has not been disclosed to Universal, and CFIA has provided no satisfactory explanation for the discrepancy."

items: Nearly $7M of taxpayer funds spent on ostrich cull in Edgewood, B.C., data reveals

blocks.text: Diet pill 'on the cusp' of launching
The court filing says the couple were never compensated for 1,200 ostrich eggs allegedly seized by the CFIA as part of the culling operation.
"The eggs have not been returned. CFIA has provided no justification for the retention or disposition of the eggs" the claim reads.
Those eggs, it goes on to say, formed part of a "commercial enterprise" which included the development of a dietary supplement pill that the farm was "on the cusp" of launching.
The company claims the venture was projected to generate $200 million in revenue.
"CFIA bears liability in negligence for the full measure of this commercial loss," the document says.
The claim against the CFIA and RCMP includes allegations of cruelty towards the farm's ostriches in the lead-up to the mass cull. (Aaron Hemens/Canadian Press)
Espersen and Bilinski have previously stated their farm pivoted from meat production to scientific research during the COVID-19 pandemic.
A close examination of scientific claims made by Espersen and Bilinski through their company Struthio Bioscience Inc, was carried out by the CBC's fifth estate earlier this year.

It revealed discrepancies and exaggerations, and included an interview with ostrich antibody researcher Yasuhiro Tsukamoto, who said plans to use the ostrich eggs to mass-produce antibodies for weight-loss supplements were called off once the flock became exposed to avian flu.

That investigation also found that over a three-year period, courts had ordered Espersen and Bilinski and their companies to pay creditors nearly $500,000, money Bilinski said they intended to pay back.
Allegations of animal cruelty, trespass
The claim against the CFIA and RCMP also includes allegations of cruelty towards the farm's ostriches by CFIA personnel in the lead-up to the cull.
"The manner in which animals were handled, quarantined, and destroyed was contrary to applicable law [and] contrary to CFIA's own operational guidelines on humane handling," it says.
Complaints against the RCMP include an allegation that officers occupied the farm "24 hours a day without consent" between Sept. 22 and Nov. 13, 2025.
The CFIA and RCMP have 21 days to respond to the claim.
In a statement provided to CBC News, the CFIA said it was aware of the lawsuit and would respond in due course.
The B.C. RCMP was also contacted but did not provide comment before deadline.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Ruby Cornish is a journalist with CBC News based in Vancouver. She spent more than a decade reporting, producing and presenting with Australia's public broadcaster before relocating to Canada in 2026.

"If we allowed Iran to have a nuclear weapon, this country could never function the same way," he argued.
Oil prices dropped significantly as the US and Iran renewed the talks over ending the war between the two countries.
The midterms are largely seen as a referendum on the current US president's policies.
The Democrats are expected to retake the House of Representatives from the Republicans' control, but the fight for the Senate is considered to be close.

articles.title: Canadian dentist detained by ICE in Minnesota ordered released by federal judge
articles.summary: A Canadian dentist detained by U.S. federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Minnesota during a green card interview has been ordered released by a federal judge.

image.caption: A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) vehicle seen in New Jersey. A federal judge ordered the release of a Canadian dentist detained by ICE in Minnesota last month, saying his constitutional rights were violated. (Shannon Stapleton/Reuters)

blocks.text: Canada·New
A Canadian dentist detained by U.S. federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Minnesota during a green card interview has been ordered released by a federal judge.
Dr. William Lizardo was arrested Oct. 23 at a green card interview
U.S. District Judge Michael J. Davis wrote in his ruling that the arrest and detention of Dr. William Lizardo, 32, originally of Mississauga, Ont., violated his constitutional rights.

Lizardo moved to the U.S. on a student visa in 2019 to study at the University of Minnesota School of Dentistry, according to court documents. He graduated in 2023 and married an American that same year. They had a daughter two years later.

Lizardo's wife filed a petition for an alien relative in September 2023, while Lizardo applied to adjust his status to permanent residency. The relative petition was approved in January 2025, according to the court.

Lizardo practiced dentistry in federally-designated shortage areas until his work authorization was revoked, at which time he started volunteering at a low-cost clinic in Burnsville, Minn., according to the court documents.
New bodycam video shows aftermath of ICE shooting in NYC

In January, his request for permanent residency was denied because he had failed to provide a certfied document from Ontario. Orders to appear at subsequent hearings were sent to the wrong address. Lizardo missed the hearings and was subsequently arrested by ICE Oct. 23, detained at Sherburne County Jail, and ordered removed from the U.S.

The judge called the facts of the case "appalling" — noting that while the couple moved several times, each time Lizardo "filed changes of address with the post office and with USCIS [U.S. Citizen and Immigration Services]. In turn, USCIS communicated with Petitioner at each new address."
The judge also noted that Lizardo had never been arrested during his time in the U.S.

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
Edmonton-born man held for months in ICE detention centres returns to Canada

blocks.text: Lizardo filed to have the order of removal rescinded as he had never received the notices for the hearings. That request was granted by an immigration court on Oct. 28 after it found he had provided sufficient evidence of lack of notice.
ICE argued Lizardo should be kept in custody while the green card case was being decided.
The judge ruled ICE agents had no reason to believe Lizardo was a flight risk and ordered him immediately released.

"Because the facts presented here are so appalling and so well supported, the Court could issue a long order, complete with colorful details about, and commentary on, the abuses suffered by Petitioner," the judge wrote. Instead, he said he simply wanted to make sure Lizardo didn't spend another night in jail.

articles.title: Trump’s DoJ charges six more people in ‘voter fraud’ crackdown in California
articles.summary:
Latest arrests come after DoJ unsuccessfully fought to force state election officials to set aside about 20,000 ballots

The US Department of Justice (DoJ) in California has charged six more…

blocks.text: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) in California has charged six more people with alleged voter fraud crimes, an escalation of the Trump administration’s campaign against the state’s election processes on the eve of the midterms.

Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Los Angeles and a close ally of the president, announced on Monday that his office was prosecuting six lawful permanent residents accused of unlawfully registering to vote and casting fraudulent ballots. The DoJ filed similar charges against 28 people across California last month and arranged for a dramatic on-camera arrest of one 72-year-old defendant, editing the footage into a DoJ promotional video.
The six new defendants are all green card holders, according to criminal complaints filed in federal court, meaning they are immigrants who have legal status, but are barred from voting.
Voting by noncitizens is extremely rare, and experts say when noncitizens do end up on the voter rolls, it is usually due to confusion.

The latest arrests come as the DoJ pushes ahead with its lawsuit seeking to force California election officials to set aside roughly 20,000 ballots that federal prosecutors say may belong to noncitizens who fraudulently registered. The DoJ has said the ballots should not be counted until California can confirm their citizenship status. State election leaders have countered that prosecutors’ list and methodology was unreliable and that complying with the demands in the middle of an election would be logistically impossible and would risk disenfranchising US citizens. Multiple judges have rebuffed the DoJ’s efforts as unconstitutional and a threat to democracy, and the US supreme court on Monday rejected the Trump administration’s appeals.

Five of the six people charged in the latest round of prosecutions have been arrested, Essayli said at a press conference on Monday. The six defendants include people originally from Mexico, Israel, the Philippines, Canada and Iran, prosecutors said.

All six are accused of a single charge each of making false statements on a naturalization application, with affidavits alleging they unlawfully registered to vote, and then when they later applied for citizenship, they falsely claimed that they had never previously registered. The complaints said the defendants cast ballots in recent years, but they are not facing charges specifically relating to fraudulently voting.

The defendants are facing a maximum of five years in prison, according to prosecutors. The charges were outlined in initial complaints written by Department of Homeland Security (DHS) agents. The defendants have not been formally indicted, and it was not immediately clear if any of them had obtained lawyers. The federal public defender’s office in Los Angeles did not immediately respond to an inquiry.

One 52-year-old defendant from Canada was accused of voting unlawfully twice, then seeking to cancel his registration. The complaint says he has been in the US for more than 40 years. A 43-year-old defendant from the Philippines has been in the US since 1992 and was accused of voting several times since 2020.

Experts have said it was extraordinary for the DoJ to bring these cases in the middle of an election, with federal prosecutors traditionally avoiding taking steps that could be seen as politically motivated or potential interference with an upcoming race. Former prosecutors and defense lawyers have said it was especially galling to see the government present the arrests in such a showy manner, blasting mugshots and parading defendants in front of news cameras.

The Associated Press and other news outlets were present for a pre-dawn arrest of the 72-year-old last month on a quiet residential street, and a Fox News reporter on Monday posted photos of two arrests, including one who appeared to be an Amazon worker handcuffed on the sidewalk. Democrats have accused the DoJ of trying to sow doubt in the results of the election and create a false impression that voter fraud is widespread.

Essayli said the newly arrested defendants were on federal prosecutors’ list of 20,000 voters who might be fraudulently registered, arguing the cases further supported their push to stop ballots from being counted. But an immigrants’ rights group, which sued the government over its use of federal immigration data to challenge voters, analyzed the list and said in a filing over the weekend that more than 40% of the people flagged as potentially fraudulent voters could not be found on the state’s voter rolls.
The 20,000 names represent a tiny fraction of the more than 23 million registered voters in California.
County election officials who have received threatening letters from the DoJ with demands that they set aside certain ballots have also said the lists handed to them were riddled with errors.

When questioned about the prosecutors’ list on Monday, Essayli told reporters the government had used “third-party databases” to identify potentially fraudulent voters, and that it “may not be 100%” accurate, but there was a “very, very high confidence rate”. At a press briefing during the first round of arrests last month, Trent McCotter, the acting US deputy attorney general, said: “There may be some names on there who, it turns out, ultimately are citizens. We’re not perfect, and that’s why we’ve asked California to cooperate with us.”

The DoJ in recent days has also repeatedly threatened to criminally prosecute election officials who process fraudulent ballots, prompting a rebuke from a federal judge on Friday, who said the DoJ’s “intimidation, threats, and attempts at coercion force election workers daily to choose between acceding to [the DoJ’s] unlawful demands or adhering to their duties and thereby subjecting themselves to a serious risk of criminal investigation and prosecution”. The judge blocked the administration from continuing to threaten election officials.

Essayli has continued his crusade against California’s elections even after a federal judge ruled last week that he was “unlawfully” serving as the head of the US attorney’s office since he was not formally appointed and confirmed by the Senate. The DoJ is appealing that ruling.

items: Sam Levine contributed reporting

articles.title: Privacy watchdog urges Senate to further amend Liberals' controversial lawful access bill
articles.summary: After facing searing criticism this spring, the Liberal government's hot-button lawful access legislation — which would make it easier for Canadian police and intelligence officials to tap private…

image.caption: Privacy Commissioner of Canada Philippe Dufresne says further amendments to the Liberals' lawful access bill are needed. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

After facing searing criticism this spring, the Liberal government's hot-button lawful access legislation — which would make it easier for Canadian police and intelligence officials to tap private communications — now begins its time before a Senate committee.
Bill C-22 begins Senate committee study after passing House in June

Canada's privacy watchdog is urging the Senate to further amend the Liberal government's hot-button lawful access legislation — which would make it easier for Canadian police and intelligence officials to tap private communications.

The Senate's national security committee is beginning its review of Bill C-22, which would give law enforcement agencies and the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (CSIS) faster access to digital information during investigations — something the community has been pushing for decades.
While Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree brought in amendments in June, the bill continues to face pushback.

"Extra amendments, I believe, are still necessary to better protect the privacy of Canadians while continuing to provide to state authorities the tools needed to carry out their important work," Privacy Commissioner Philippe Dufresne testified in French late Monday afternoon.

items: Conservatives blast Liberals for trying to 'ram' through C-22
Liberals to amend police data interception bill following searing criticism

blocks.text: If it passes, the bill would lower the legal threshold for law enforcement and intelligence bodies to access basic subscriber information — like names, addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses and account numbers — from "reasonable grounds to believe" down to "reasonable grounds to suspect" that an offence has been or will be committed.
Dufresne said the definition of subscriber information and who can be asked to hand it over remain overly broad relative to the lowered threshold required to access it.

"Depending on the nature of the services in question (which could include health-care providers, lawyers, financial institutions and dating apps), such information could reasonably attract a heightened expectation of privacy due to its sensitivity," he said.

The commissioner recommended narrowing the definition of subscriber information to a finite list or adding a carve-out for medical or privileged information to protection orders and limiting the requests only to telecommunications service providers.
While the bill would clarify that police do not require a warrant for "any information that is available to the public," Dufresne said the concept of "publicly available" information is undefined.
"An individual does not automatically forfeit any reasonable expectation of privacy in information that has become public," he argued.
Bill C-22 needed, argues minister

The second half of the bill has attracted the most objections. It would force tech companies to adapt their systems so they all have the ability to hand over information to investigators with a warrant.

Bill C-22 also grants the minister the authority to issue confidential ministerial orders to electronic service providers (ESPs) operating in Canada, requiring them to build surveillance and monitoring capabilities into their systems. Orders would first be reviewed from the intelligence commissioner — an independent quasi-judicial official.
The government has argued secrecy is needed to avoid tipping off threat actors — but companies have argued that limits their ability to object.

Intelligence Commissioner Simon Noël told senators on the committee they might want to consider whether the bill should explicitly require the minister to consider necessity and proportionality when making order.

"If the intent of ministerial orders is to respond to situations where confidentiality is necessary, a clear proportionality factor that includes reasonable alternatives would ensure the minister explains the needs," he said.
Some of the main criticism of Bill C-22 comes from tech and communications companies who argue it would force them to introduce backdoors.

Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree says law enforcement and intelligence agencies need platforms to have the ability to quickly provide the information they seek. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)
Before the bill was sent to the Senate in June, Anandasangaree brought in amendments that put limits on when companies would be required to decrypt information.

Another change reduces the length of time that tech companies would have to retain metadata to six months from up to a year, after cybersecurity experts warned that data would be an attractive target for hackers.
One of the bill's critics, tech giant Apple, maintains the amendments don't go far enough.

"While we appreciate attempts to improve C-22, the bill could still undermine Apple's ability to offer the powerful privacy and security features our users expect from us, including encryption, even as AI and other evolving technologies provide hackers with new tools to exploit cybersecurity weaknesses," it said in a statement earlier this month.

Testifying before the same Senate committee later Monday, Anandasangaree argued investigators face delays in obtaining basic information that may be critical to identifying a suspect or rescuing a victim.
"That is why Bill C-22 matters," he said.

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump bid to block 20,000 California ballots
articles.summary: The Trump administration had appealed to the Supreme Court over claims that a list of more than 20,000 ballots in California include non-US citizens.

image.caption: Early voting has been underway in California since October Image: Mario Tama/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: On the eve of the US midterm elections, the administration of President Donald Trump made a last ditch attempt to sideline over 20,000 mail-in ballots in California, claiming non-US citizens are attempting to vote.
The US Justice Department (DoJ), which is run by Trump's former personal attorney Todd Blanche, has claimed to have a list documenting non-US citizens on California's voter rolls.
In mid October, the federal government first filed a lawsuit based on the allegations, which was rejected by a California district court.
On Monday, the DoJ asked for a "limited injunction" directing the state of California to "stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones" pending the verification of voters' status.
However, hours after the appeal was filed, the Supreme Court said it would decline to stop California from counting the votes.

When the initial lawsuit was filed by the Trump administration earlier in October, Los Angeles District Judge David Carter had warned that singling out ballots would "wreak havoc" on the election process and harm voters' trust in the democratic process.
"If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," Carter wrote in rejecting the initial suit.
Early voting has been underway in California for several weeks, with hundreds of thousands of ballots already processed.
Battle for US midterm elections heats up
Analysis shows thousands of eligible voters on ballot blacklist

The voter list had been compiled by the US Department of Homeland Security. In its response to the federal government's lawsuit, California defended its election integrity, and said the process used by the Trump administration to identify non-citizen voters was likely flawed and full of errors.
Last week, another federal judge ordered the DoJ to share its list with an immigrant rights group, and a voting rights watchdog based out of the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).

A legal filing of the analysis found that thousands of US citizens on the list appear to be inexplicably flagged as ineligible to vote. US District Judge Carter said people recently flagged as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalised US citizens.
Trump's fixation on voter fraud
Trump has made unfounded claims of election fraud for years, despite multiple investigations finding such malfeasance is exceedingly rare.
For the current midterm election cycle, Trump has zeroed in on claiming non US citizens are trying to vote, despite these claims being repeatedly debunked by research and investigation.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own ​constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," US District Judge Carter wrote in October.
The most populous US state, California, leans heavily Democratic, and is not expected to be a competitive state for Trump's Republicans in the midterms.
California governor Gavin Newsom is an outspoken critic of Trump, and has warned the president's administration against trying to interfere in the state's voting process.

Ahead of the midterm voting on Tuesday, Newsom announced the deployment of election law experts, poll observers and a help line for voters to report any attempts of intimidation or interference at the polls.
What could a Democrat win mean for Trump's presidency?

articles.title: Supreme court rules against Trump over bid to force California to set aside ballots
articles.summary:
Justice department had ordered state to segregate and not count 20,000 ballots from people it claims are non-citizens

The supreme court on Monday ruled against the Trump administration and…

blocks.text: The supreme court on Monday ruled against the Trump administration and its attempts to force California election officials to segregate and not count ballots from people that the justice department claims are non-citizens. The ruling follows several lower courts siding with California officials, who argued the federal government was seeking to interfere in state elections.

California and the Trump administration have been in a legal standoff over the past few weeks following the justice department’s claim that 20,000 non-citizens were on the state’s voter rolls. The DoJ delivered a USB drive to Los Angeles and Sacramento election officials in mid-October with the names, giving only 48 hours for officials to review the list and threatening to sue if the ballots were not sequestered until those listed could verify their citizenship. Election officials refused, leading to a series of courtroom battles.

The justice department’s claims faced immediate pushback from state officials and voting rights groups, who questioned how the agency compiled the list and accused the Trump administration of a ploy to cast doubt over midterm elections. The justice department refused to provide details on its methodology and analysis from election officials found numerous suggestions the list contained inaccuracies.

“The Department of Justice has not provided the underlying evidence, source, or methodology supporting its assertions that individuals identified in its records are ineligible to vote,” Dean Logan, Los Angeles county clerk and recorder, said in a statement after receiving the list.

The fight between the Trump administration and California officials escalated over recent weeks and subsequent court rulings. The administration has threatened to prosecute election officials if they process ineligible non-citizen ballots, a move experts say would have no legal basis. The Trump administration has also opened a criminal investigation in California to pursue claims of non-citizen voting, as well as begun subpoenaing election officials.

US district judge David Carter previously rebuffed the administration’s request to segregate ballots in a ruling on 28 October. Carter, who was nominated to the bench by Bill Clinton, wrote in his decision about how the administration’s move to interfere in California’s vote was unusual and extreme.

“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” Carter wrote.

The Trump administration’s demands are part of a larger effort by the federal government to assert a greater role in overseeing elections and push claims of voter fraud committed by non-citizens. The justice department has made a similar demand to segregate ballots in Washington state, while also filing criminal charges against 28 green card holders in California that the DoJ accuses of fraudulently registering to vote and casting illegal ballots.

Trump has also made vague promises to issue a $1m reward to anyone whose reports of voter fraud lead to an arrest or conviction. Data and experts have shown that ineligible non-citizen voting is extremely rare.

articles.title: Indonesia's toxic haze is giving its neighbours a political headache
articles.summary: Governments in Singapore and Malaysia are split between anxious citizens and an irascible neighbour.

blocks.text: The haze billowing out from wildfires in the Indonesian regions of Kalimantan, Papua and Sumatra knows no borders.
Carried by winds to nearby Singapore and Malaysia, the toxic smog has in recent weeks impacted populations across maritime South East Asia, triggering respiratory illnesses and headaches.
It's also giving the region's governments a different kind of headache - split between the mounting frustrations of their citizens and the risk of souring diplomatic ties with Indonesia.

"People are fed up, angry and anxious," Eugene Tan, associate professor of law at the Singapore Management University, tells the BBC. "The governments have to respond to them, or else what is more an external issue has become an internal one with ample headroom for politicisation."
Indonesia's wildfires are a yearly occurrence, widely associated with industrial-scale land clearing to make way for crops like oil palm.
But the blazes this year have been particularly difficult to tame due to a strong El Niño, which has exacerbated drought conditions in the country's forests and peatlands.
Whereas previous haze episodes in Singapore and Malaysia have typically lasted for a few days, this time it stretched into weeks.

In Malaysia, locals started a boycott of Indonesian products in protest against the haze, after lawmaker Syed Saddiq called for sanctions on companies linked to the wildfires and said Malaysians should "treat them as an outcast in the region".
There have also been complaints in Singapore, a country that has come to expect seamless efficiency from its leaders.

"There appears to be the view that the government dropped the ball in dealing with the haze, given that it was known that the El Niño weather phenomenon would be severe and that early warning was given," says Tan.
"Clearly, Singaporeans expect the government to decisively deal with the polluters."
As the haze spiralled into yet another crisis for Prabowo's beleaguered administration, some officials pushed back against criticism.
One senior official ruffled feathers when he said the wildfires were out of human control and that oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
That remark was "disappointing" and "not right", according to Singaporean senior minister K Shanmugam - a rare rebuke from the city state, which prides itself on its diplomatic prowess.

"The haze is affecting our health seriously, and it's really unacceptable," Shanmugam told reporters. Since the haze impacts citizens on both sides of the border, there should not be "any bilateral issues" in addressing it, he added.
"The Indonesian public is suffering as well, and it is in Indonesia's interest as much as ours to deal with the companies that are causing these problems."
Days later, Indonesia announced it would reduce gas exports to Singapore, citing domestic energy needs - a move that many saw as retaliation to Singapore's rhetoric.

To be sure, Indonesia has faced recent electricity shortages in parts of the country. Singapore also says the reduction, which amounts to less than 2% of its total daily demand, will have little impact on its gas supply.

But the abrupt announcement came just days after Indonesia's energy minister warned that they could halt gas exports to countries that don't "respect Indonesia". That same day, Prabowo made reference to "countries that like to insult Indonesia" when talking about the wildfires.

"It's a tired playbook of using Singapore as the bogeyman, driven by the 'abang-adik' [big brother-little brother] syndrome," Tan says, referring to a historical dynamic that Singapore's leaders have long tried to shrug off: the expectation that it should defer to its larger neighbours.
"Singapore leaders expressing concerns about the haze and how it affects the people of both countries have been taken to mean that Singapore has been disrespectful to its neighbour."
In contrast, Malaysia's official rhetoric on the haze has been relatively muted.
Its foreign minister Mohamad Hasan has ruled out lodging a formal diplomatic protest with Indonesia or taking legal action, saying such actions "would mean we were prepared to sever relations".
For now, Malaysia has agreed to explore a memorandum of understanding with Indonesia to strengthen wildfire prevention efforts.
It would also rely on diplomatic mechanisms, Mohamad said - like the Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
The agreement, which came into effect in 2003, commits members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to collaborate on tackling the recurring haze.
But many see it as toothless, as it is unable to punish agricultural companies linked to wildfires or to force individual governments to do so.
The agreement has turned out to be "just not worth the paper it was signed on", says James Chin, professor of Asian studies at the University of Tasmania.
"The moment the haze disappears, the moment the political pressure's off, it's back to business as usual."
In 2016, Asean countries had set a goal to eliminate haze in the region by 2020. When that deadline drifted quietly by, they set a new target of achieving the goal by 2030 instead.

Complicating Malaysia's position is the fact that it is also a major palm oil producer. The commodity is often linked to commercial "slash-and-burn" practices that are widely blamed for the region's wildfires.
Malaysia has at times dealt with acute haze stemming from blazes on local land.

In 2019, when Malaysia pointed to hotspots in Indonesia's peatlands as the cause of the haze shrouding the region, Indonesian authorities pointed the finger back at Malaysia, claiming the smog came from their side.
"As long as we place a lot of importance on oil palm planting, [the haze] is going to recur," says Ei Sun Oh, principal adviser at the Pacific Research Centre of Malaysia.

And even if Malaysia were to speak up, Oh adds, it's unlikely to wield the same "leverage" over Indonesia as Singapore, which is Indonesia's largest foreign investor and an offshore financial hub for many wealthy Indonesians.
For now, Malaysia "doesn't want to unduly provoke Indonesia", says Oh.
"The government is just wringing their hands till the wind blows [the problem] over. Because eventually it will blow over."

articles.title: Economic frustration set to boil over in U.S. midterm elections

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump dances during a campaign rally at Rock Hill Sports and Event Center, on Thursday, in Rock Hill, S.C. (Scott Kinser/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business·Analysis
The U.S. economy is booming. But as they prepare to vote in Tuesday's midterm elections, American consumers have never been more pessimistic. Economists blame tariffs and the war with Iran.
Consumer sentiment hits all-time low as Americans head to the polls
American voters are headed to the polls for the U.S. midterms this week. Most are angry and frustrated about the state of the economy and the way Donald Trump has managed it.
If you want evidence of that dissatisfaction look no further than the University of Michigan's Index of Consumer Sentiment.
It shows consumer confidence is plummetting under Trump.

"Only three times since the 1970s have more than half of Americans said their government's doing bad job managing the economy. Right now it's at 74 per cent," said Kathryn Anne Edwards, a labour economist and policy consultant in Houston.
The index gauges consumer sentiment. It is lower today than it was during the toughest recessions in the 1980s or even the financial crisis in 2008-09.
And she says that survey is one of the biggest and longest standing bodies of economic data in the country. It's been going on since the 1940s. And it's been a monthly survey since 1978.
Edwards says these kinds of numbers show that on some fundamental level, the U.S. economy is failing American households.
"It's so completely unprecedented. It's really hard to put into words," said Edwards.
Those kind of plunges in consumer sentiment historically only happen in the deepest and darkest days of a recession.
And that's what's odd.
The U.S. economy is nowhere near a recession.
The latest GDP numbers out of Washington show the U.S. economy is the fastest growing economy in the Western world.
American GDP expanded by 3.8 per cent in the quarter running from July to September. (By comparison, Canada is on track for about a third of that growth.)
Retail sales were up. Investment in AI continues to churn ever higher. And stock markets are at an all-time high.

"GDP is growing above trend, consumer spending remains robust, layoffs trudge along at ultra-low levels, and we've seen a stable unemployment rate over the past year," wrote RBC's team of economists Mike Reid, Carrie Freestone and Imri Haggin.
But if the macro data is so good, why are voters so angry?

"For many voters, the economy is now synonymous with inflation, as rising prices outweigh job reports, housing affordability and stock market performance," wrote Francis Généreux, lead economist at Desjardins Group in a note to clients.
And those rising prices have been driven by two main things; tariffs and the U.S.-led war with Iran.

Gas prices shot up the day the war began. They have bounced around a little as talk of various ceasefires and deals come and go, but American drivers are paying far more at the pumps today than they were a year ago.
And gasoline prices are posted everywhere as drivers and pedestrians alike move through a neighbourhood. So even if you ride a bicycle to work, the increase in prices is incredibly hard to ignore.
Inflation in the U.S. has ticked up to 3.7 per cent, and economists warn it's not done climbing yet.
Yes, much of that increase is due to energy costs. But tariffs have contributed as well.
A recent report from the New York Federal Reserve found the cost of many everyday items would have declined last year were it not for Trump's tariffs.
Researchers looked at the 12-month change in consumer goods prices going back to the peak of the COVID-era surge in inflation. They showed price growth was still falling in 2024 and reversed in 2025.

"Our estimates attribute this increase to the tariffs: by February 2026, tariffs had contributed 2.9 percentage points to goods price inflation, and without them goods prices would have fallen slightly," wrote Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise and David E. Weinstein.

And Edwards says voters have followed the Trump administration's policy decisions and how they drive prices. She says there are two sharp drops in the consumer sentiment index. One when tariffs were introduced and the other when the war with Iran began.
"Americans get it. Tariffs have made their lives more expensive," she said.

And Americans will take that knowledge into the polling booth this week. If the polls hold, the midterms could lead to sweeping changes in the formation of Congress and who holds power on Capitol Hill.
But whether those newly elected Senate and House members actually take action to lower tariffs for Canadians is a different question altogether.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Armstrong is the CBC's senior business correspondent. He was a foreign correspondent and a parliamentary reporter for CBC News. Peter hosted the business program On the Money and World Report on CBC Radio. He is the author of the CBC newsletter Mind Your Business
